own_scenes.desc: Al final de 1966 el LSD llevó al pop de vuelta a la infancia y a la locura. Los Beatles empezaron el 24 de noviembre «Strawberry Fields Forever», un viaje de Lennon hacia abajo, no hacia atrás, al orfanato junto a su casa, «psicoanálisis con música», unida por Geoff Emerick a partir de dos tomas; luego «When I’m Sixty-Four» y «Penny Lane». En Navidad la BBC aplazó el Alice in Wonderland de Jonathan Miller, sin cabezas de animal, con el sitar de Ravi Shankar y rodado en un hospital militar de víctimas de neurosis de guerra: un catálogo de psicosis. Grace Slick llevó «White Rabbit» a Jefferson Airplane; Syd Barrett escribía sobre el mundo de Lewis Carroll. Proliferaban los discos sobre la locura («They’re Coming to Take Me Away, Ha-Haaa!», «Pandora’s Golden Heebie Jeebies» de los Association), y en el corazón secreto del año, la tristeza frágil de «How Can We Hang On to a Dream» de Tim Hardin.

influences.name: San Francisco: Acid Tests y Haight-Ashbury

refs.q: It was, as Lennon would say the next year, ‘psychoanalysis set to music’
refs.para: It was, as Lennon would say the next year, ‘psychoanalysis set to music’, the beginning of his desire to explore the innermost recesses of his soul. ‘Strawberry Fields Forever’ was couched in hallucinatory perception and existential riddles that echoed his favourite childhood reading, Lewis Carroll’s Alice in Wonderland: as Alice wondered, ‘Let me think, was I the same when I got up this morning? I almost think I can remember feeling a little different. But if I’m not the same, the next question is, “Who in the world am I?”’
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: Like ‘Strawberry Fields Forever’, Miller’s Alice in Wonderland was at once disorienting
refs.para: Like ‘Strawberry Fields Forever’, Miller’s Alice in Wonderland was at once disorienting – eliding the distinctions between dream and reality, adulthood and childhood – and psychologically acute, accurately representing the way that dreams process daily events into a parallel life that, although fantastical, has its own logic and meaning. As Alfred Hitchcock once said, ‘When you dream, you dream very real. Very real. Everything seems real in a dream. You are glad to wake up, because it’s so real. So, you take a dream idea – it’s a nightmare – and you make it real.’
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: Indeed, December 1966 saw yet more records with madness as a theme.
refs.para: Indeed, December 1966 saw yet more records with madness as a theme. It had begun with ‘19th Nervous Breakdown’ and the summer’s improbable novelty hit, Napoleon XIV’s ‘They’re Coming to Take Me Away, Ha Ha’, a rewrite of Dylan’s off-kilter ‘Rainy Day Women #12 and 35’. As well as Mick Softley’s Revolver-inspired ‘Am I the Red One’ – chromatic riddles worthy of Alice – there was the gibbering paranoia of ‘The Shadow Chasers’ by the Freaks of Nature and the full-blown freak-out of the Move’s ‘Disturbance’.
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia
